examples.problem:
The diagram below shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. If the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $\left(3,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and $m \angle AOB=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ what are the Cartesian coordinates of $B?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13952748/assets/a0d06318ba26eee754bc3581f5a0f1c126eb0723f8aea2cac0fad075ee56e7f9.png)
examples.worked_solution:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $\left(3,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right),$ we must have $r=3.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $3,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $3.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle counterclockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta$-coordinate of $A$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ the $\theta$-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
\theta_B = \dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $\left(3,\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		x &= r\cos\theta\[5pt]
		 &=3\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \right)\[5pt]
		 &=3\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
		 &=-\dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{2}
	}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		y &= r\sin\theta\[5pt]
		 &= 3\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \right)\[5pt]
		 &= 3\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\[5pt]
		 &=\dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{2}
	}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $\left(-\dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{2}\right).$

feedback.problem:
The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,\frac{\pi }{6})$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(\frac{r}{3},\frac{5\pi }{6}).$ Determine the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(\sqrt{3},1).$

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find $r,$ the distance between $A$ and the origin:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(\frac{2}{3},\frac{5\pi }{6}).$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3},\frac{1}{3}).$
